l: Deity Heavenly-Bird-Boat, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Deity Heavenly-Bird-Boat was attached to Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity and sent with him to the little shore of Inasa. He helped summon Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master and participated in asking Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land to yield the Central Land of Reed-Plains.

l: Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land was asked to yield the Central Land of Reed-Plains to the august child of the Heavenly Deities. After consulting his sons and hearing their agreement, he consented to yield the land in exchange for the establishment of a great abode for himself and respectful service to his children.

l: Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master was summoned from Cape Miho and told Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land that he would respectfully present the land to the august child of the Heavenly Deity. He then disappeared after overturning his boat and clapping his heavenly departing hands in a fence of green branches.

l: Deity Brave-August-Name-Firm, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Deity Brave-August-Name-Firm came bearing a thousand-draught rock and demanded a trial of strength with Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity. After his hand was first turned into an icicle and then a sword-blade, his hand was crushed, he fled, and he agreed to obey his father's command and yield the Central Land of Reed-Plains.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The august child of the Heavenly Deities was designated to govern the Central Land of Reed-Plains. Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land agreed to yield the land according to the command of the august child of the Heavenly Deities.

l: Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Central Land of Reed-Plains was the dominion that the Heavenly Deities commanded Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land to yield to the august child of the Heavenly Deities. Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land and his sons agreed that it would be yielded.

l: Land of Idzumo, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The little shore of Inasa and the shore of Tagishi were in the land of Idzumo. The heavenly august abode for Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land was built on the shore of Tagishi in the land of Idzumo.

l: dominion of the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The dominion of the Central Land of Reed-Plains was the dominion that the Heavenly Deities charged the august child with governing.

l: abdication of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The abdication of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land occurred after his sons agreed to follow the commands of the august child of the Heavenly Deities. He yielded the Central Land of Reed-Plains while requesting that a great abode be established for him and that Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master respectfully serve his children.

l: trial of strength, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The trial of strength began when Deity Brave-August-Name-Firm asked to take Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity's hand. Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity prevailed by crushing Deity Brave-August-Name-Firm's hand, causing him to flee and submit.

l: yielding up the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The yielding up the Central Land of Reed-Plains was agreed to by Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master, Deity Brave-August-Name-Firm, and Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land. It was made according to the command of the august child of the Heavenly Deities.

l: subduing and pacifying the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Subduing and pacifying the Central Land of Reed-Plains was reported by Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity after Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land and his sons agreed to yield the land.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity and the High-Integrity-Deity charge His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven and rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains after its pacification. At the eight-forking road of Heaven, the Deity Prince of Saruta identifies himself as an Earthly Deity and offers to serve as the august child's vanguard. The deities send down the mirror, sword, and other divine attendants with His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty and instruct him on their reverence and governance.

l: Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, together with the High-Integrity-Deity, commands His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven and rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains. Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity also helps question the radiant Deity at the eight-forking road of Heaven and joins the mirror and other divine objects to the descent.

l: His Augustness Truly-Conquer-I-Conqueror-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Truly-Conqueror-I-Conquer-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears reports that a child, His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, has been born and should be sent down in his place.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty is charged to rule the Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears and agrees to descend from Heaven. He receives the mirror, the Herb-Quelling-Great-Sword, and several deities, and is instructed to regard the mirror as the august spirit of the commanding deities.

l: Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears is identified as the land over which His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty shall rule.

l: Heavenly-Alarming-Female, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Heavenly-Alarming-Female-Deity is commanded to question the Deity whose refulgence reaches from the Plain of High Heaven to the Central Land of Reed-Plains. She asks who he is and later descends among the five chiefs of companies.

l: Deity Prince of Saruta, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Deity Prince of Saruta identifies himself as an Earthly Deity at the eight-forking road of Heaven. He says he has come to meet the august child of the Heavenly Deities and offer himself as His Augustness's vanguard.

l: mirror, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The mirror that had allured the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity from the Rock-Dwelling is joined to His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty for his descent. He is instructed to regard the mirror exactly as the august spirit of the commanding deities and to reverence it accordingly.

l: Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Central Land of Reed-Plains is described as having been pacified by the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity. It is the land to which His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty is sent to dwell in and rule.

l: eight-forking road of Heaven, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The eight-forking road of Heaven is the place where a Deity's refulgence reaches upward to the Plain of High Heaven and downward to the Central Land of Reed-Plains. The Deity Prince of Saruta stands there to meet the descending august child.

l: Heaven, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Heaven is the place from which His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty is commanded to descend. The eight-forking road of Heaven is also associated with the passage between Heaven and the Central Land of Reed-Plains.

l: August Descent from Heaven of His Augustness the August Grandchild, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The August Descent from Heaven of His Augustness the August Grandchild concerns the command for His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven and rule the Luxuriant Reed-Plain-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears. It includes the questioning of the Deity Prince of Saruta and the sending of divine objects and attendants with the august child.

l: subduing and pacifying the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The pacification of the Central Land of Reed-Plains is reported as completed by the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity. After this pacification, the deities arrange for His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend and rule the land.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity and High-Integrating-Deity commanded His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven. He descended onto the peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsu-kushi, while His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness and His Augustness Heaven's-Round-Eyes attended him in his august van. His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness declared the place exceedingly good and then established a dwelling there with stout temple-pillars and high cross-beams.

l: Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity commanded His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven.

l: High-Integrating-Deity, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: High-Integrating-Deity commanded His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty to descend from Heaven.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty left the Heavenly Rock-Seat, parted the heavenly clouds, and descended from Heaven onto the peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsu-kushi.

l: peak of Kuzhifuru, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsu-kushi, was where His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty descended from Heaven.

l: His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness attended His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty in his august van with Heavenly weapons. He said that the place was exceedingly good, established temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom, raised the cross-beams to the Plain of High Heaven, and dwelt there.

l: Heaven, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Heaven was the place from which His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty descended.

l: descent from Heaven, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The descent from Heaven brought His Augustness Heaven's-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty onto the peak of Kuzhifuru, which is Takachiho in Tsu-kushi.

l: dwelling at Takachiho, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Dwelling at Takachiho was established after His Heavenly Great Wondrous Augustness judged the place exceedingly good. He made stout the temple-pillars on the nethermost rock-bottom and made high the cross-beams to the Plain of High Heaven.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The unit concerns Her Augustness the Heavenly-Alarming-Female and the Great Deity Prince of Saruta. She is charged with respectfully escorting the Great Deity Prince of Saruta back, because she had made him known. She is also charged with bearing his august name and serving the speaker. As a result, the Duchesses of Saru bear the name of the Male Deity the Prince of Saruta, and the women are called Duchesses of Saru.

l: Heavenly-Alarming-Female, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Heavenly-Alarming-Female is charged with respectfully escorting the Great Deity Prince of Saruta back. She is also charged with bearing his august name and respectfully serving the speaker.

l: Deity Prince of Saruta, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Great Deity Prince of Saruta respectfully served as the speaker's august vanguard. The Heavenly-Alarming-Female had made him known and is charged with escorting him back.

l: Duchesses of Saru, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Duchesses of Saru bear the name of the Male Deity the Prince of Saruta. The women are called Duchesses of Saru.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The unit concerns the Deity Prince of Saruta while he dwells at Azaka. He goes fishing, is caught by a hirabu shell-fish, and drowns in the sea, receiving three names associated with sinking, gurgling water, and bubbles. The Heavenly-Alarming-Female escorts him back and asks the fishes to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities. All the fishes agree except the bèche-de-mer, whose mouth she slits; this explains its slit mouth and the offerings granted to the Duchesses of Saru.

l: Deity Prince of Saruta, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Deity Prince of Saruta dwells at Azaka and goes fishing. A hirabu shell-fish catches his hand, and he drowns in the sea, where he receives three names associated with sinking, gurgling water, and bubbles.

l: Azaka, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Azaka is where the Deity Prince of Saruta dwells when he goes fishing.

l: Heavenly-Alarming-Female, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Heavenly-Alarming-Female escorts the Deity Prince of Saruta back. She gathers the fishes, asks them to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities, and slits the mouth of the bèche-de-mer when it gives no reply.

l: fishes, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The fishes, both broad of fin and narrow of fin, are gathered and asked to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities. They declare that they will respectfully serve him, except for the bèche-de-mer.

l: bèche-de-mer, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The bèche-de-mer gives no reply when the fishes are asked to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deities. The Heavenly-Alarming-Female slits its mouth with a stiletto, explaining why it has a slit mouth at the present day.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty met Divine-Princess-of-Ata, daughter of Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor, and sought to marry her. Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor sent both Divine-Princess-of-Ata and Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks, but His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty rejected Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks because she was very hideous and kept only Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees. Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor declared that rejecting Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks caused the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity to be as frail as flowers rather than immovable like rocks. The curse explains why the august lives of Their Augustnesses the Heavenly Sovereigns are not long.

l: The Curse of the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: It concerns the consequence of rejecting Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks and keeping only Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees. It explains why the august lives of Their Augustnesses the Heavenly Sovereigns are not long.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: He met Divine-Princess-of-Ata and asked to marry her. He rejected Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks because she was very hideous, kept only Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, and thereby caused the consequence declared by Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor.

l: Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: He was the father of Divine-Princess-of-Ata and Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks. He sent both daughters to His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, then declared that rejecting Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks would make the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity as frail as flowers.

l: Divine-Princess-of-Ata, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: She met His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty at the august cape of Kasasa. She identified herself as a daughter of Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor and was sent to His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty with her elder sister.

l: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: She was another name for Divine-Princess-of-Ata and was sent by Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor together with Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks. His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty kept her and wedded her for one night.

l: Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: She was the elder sister of Divine-Princess-of-Ata and was sent with her to His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty. He sent her back because she was very hideous, although Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor had offered her so that the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity might live eternally immovable like enduring rocks.

l: the Heavenly Sovereigns, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Their august lives are said not to be long as a consequence of Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks being sent back and only Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees being kept.

l: the august lives of Their Augustnesses the Heavenly Sovereigns, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: They are described as not long. Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor attributes this to the rejection of Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks and the keeping of Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees tells His Augustness Prince Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty that she is pregnant and near delivery. He doubts that the unborn child is his, so she tests whether the child is of a Heavenly Deity by building a sealed hall and setting it on fire during delivery. Three Deities are born in the fire: His Augustness Fire-Shine, His Augustness Fire-Climax, and His Augustness Fire-Subside, also called His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears.

l: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees tells His Augustness Prince Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty that she is pregnant and nearing delivery. She builds a hall without doors, seals its entrance with earth, and sets it on fire before giving birth.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Prince Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty is told by Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees that she is pregnant after one night. He doubts that the unborn child is his and says it must be the child of an Earthly Deity.

l: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees's unborn child, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees's unborn child is presented as either the child of an Earthly Deity or the august child of the Heavenly Deity. Its identity is tested through the circumstances of the delivery in the burning hall.

l: the delivery of Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The delivery of Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees takes place inside a hall that she has sealed and set on fire. Three Deities are born during it.

l: the hall built for the delivery, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The hall built for the delivery is eight fathoms long and has no doors. Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees seals its entrance with earth and sets it on fire before giving birth.

l: fire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Fire burns the hall during the delivery of Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees. The three Deities are born while the fire is burning, with His Augustness Fire-Shine born when it burns most fiercely.

l: His Augustness Fire-Shine, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine is the first child born in the fire, arriving when the fire is burning most fiercely. He is identified as the ancestor of the Hayabito, Dukes of Ata.

l: His Augustness Fire-Climax, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Climax is the second child born during the delivery in the burning hall.

l: His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside is the third child born during the delivery in the burning hall. He is also called His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears is another name for His Augustness Fire-Subside. He is the third of the three Deities born in the fire.

l: the three Deities born in the fire, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The three Deities born in the fire are His Augustness Fire-Shine, His Augustness Fire-Climax, and His Augustness Fire-Subside. His Augustness Fire-Subside is also called His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine and His Augustness Fire-Subside exchange their sea-luck and mountain-luck, but Fire-Subside loses Fire-Shine’s fish-hook and cannot replace it. Fire-Subside travels to the palace of the Ocean-Possessor, marries Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, and obtains the original fish-hook after the Sea-Deity finds it in the throat of the tahi. The Ocean-Possessor gives Fire-Subside instructions and two jewels for controlling the tides, and a one-fathom crocodile escorts him home.

l: His Augustness Fire-Shine, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine is a prince whose luck is on the sea, where he catches things broad of fin and narrow of fin. He exchanges luck with his younger brother but later demands the original fish-hook back after Fire-Subside loses it.

l: His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside is a prince whose luck is on the mountains, where he catches things rough of hair and soft of hair. After losing his elder brother’s fish-hook, he travels to the palace of the Ocean-Possessor, marries Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, retrieves the hook, and receives instructions and tide-controlling jewels.

l: Great-Ocean-Possessor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Deity Ocean-Possessor receives Fire-Subside at his palace, gives him Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess in marriage, and summons the fishes to locate the lost fish-hook. He instructs Fire-Subside how to return the hook and gives him the tide-flowing jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel.

l: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess is the daughter of the Sea-Deity and becomes delighted when she sees Fire-Subside. She tells her father about Fire-Subside’s sigh, and she is given in marriage to him.

l: the elder-younger brother relationship, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine is the elder brother and His Augustness Fire-Subside is the younger brother. Fire-Subside repeatedly asks to exchange luck with Fire-Shine, later faces his brother’s urgent demand for the original fish-hook, and is instructed to counter his brother’s actions with differing field levels and tide control.

l: the exchange of luck, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine and His Augustness Fire-Subside mutually exchange their sea-luck and mountain-luck after repeated requests. Fire-Subside cannot succeed with the sea-luck and loses the fish-hook, while Fire-Shine’s luck is said to be distinct from his brother’s.

l: fish-hook, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The fish-hook belonging to His Augustness Fire-Shine is lost by His Augustness Fire-Subside while he is using the sea-luck. Fire-Subside makes hundreds and then a thousand replacement hooks, but Fire-Shine refuses them and insists on the original; the original is later found in the tahi’s throat.

l: the sea, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The sea is the realm in which His Augustness Fire-Shine has his luck and where Fire-Subside loses the fish-hook. It contains the savoury august road, the palace of the Ocean-Possessor, the fishes, and the crocodiles.

l: the palace of the Ocean-Possessor, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The palace of the Ocean-Possessor is built like fishes’ scales and lies beyond a savoury august road in the sea. Fire-Subside reaches it by boat, sits in a cassia-tree above the palace well, and stays there for three years.

l: the marriage of Fire-Subside and Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside is given Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess in marriage by her father, the Sea-Deity. Fire-Subside dwells with her in the Sea-Deity’s land for three years.

l: the lost fish-hook retrieval, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The Sea-Deity summons the fishes and learns that the tahi likely swallowed the fish-hook because it complained of something in its throat. The hook is found in the tahi’s throat, washed, and respectfully presented to His Augustness Fire-Subside.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside returns the fish-hook to his elder brother according to the Sea-Deity's instructions. The elder brother grows poorer and attacks His Augustness Fire-Subside. His Augustness Fire-Subside uses the tide-flowing jewel to drown him and the tide-ebbing jewel to save him. The elder brother then promises to guard and serve His Augustness Fire-Subside, and his drowning posturings are said to continue to the present day.

l: Submission of His Augustness Fire-Shine, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: This unit is titled “Submission of His Augustness Fire-Shine.”

l: His Augustness Fire-Shine, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Shine is named in the title of this unit.

l: His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside gives the fish-hook to his elder brother according to the Sea-Deity's instructions. When his elder brother attacks, His Augustness Fire-Subside uses the tide-flowing jewel to drown him and the tide-ebbing jewel to save him.

l: fish-hook, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The fish-hook is given to the elder brother exactly according to the Sea-Deity's words of instruction.

l: the tide-flowing jewel, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The tide-flowing jewel is used to drown the elder brother when he attacks His Augustness Fire-Subside.

l: the tide-ebbing jewel, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The tide-ebbing jewel is used to save the elder brother after he expresses grief.

l: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, daughter of the Sea-Deity, came to His Augustness Fire-Subside while pregnant and built a parturition-hall on the seashore. During parturition, she took the native shape of a crocodile, but His Augustness Fire-Subside secretly looked at her and fled. She left their august child, closed the sea-boundary, and returned to the Sea-Plain, though she later sent a song expressing love for His Augustness Fire-Subside. Their child, His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, later married Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess and had four august children.

l: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, daughter of the Sea-Deity, came to His Augustness Fire-Subside while pregnant and built a parturition-hall from cormorants' feathers. During parturition she took her native shape, which was that of a crocodile, and left after His Augustness Fire-Subside secretly looked at her. She later sent him a song through her younger sister, Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, expressing her love.

l: His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Fire-Subside was told not to look at Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess during parturition, but he stealthily peeped at her. After seeing her crocodile form, he became terrified and fled. He later received songs from Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess and replied with one expressing that he would not forget her.

l: parturition-hall, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The parturition-hall was built by Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess on the limit of the waves upon the sea-shore, using cormorants' feathers for thatch. She entered it for parturition before its thatch was completed.

l: august child of Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess and His Augustness Fire-Subside, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The august child was born to Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess during her parturition. She left the child when she returned to the Sea-Plain, and later entrusted a song to Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess on the occasion of nursing the child.

l: native shape of Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The native shape of Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess was the shape of a crocodile eight fathoms long. She took this shape during parturition.

l: crocodile, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The crocodile was the form taken by Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess during parturition. It was eight fathoms long and crawled and writhed about when His Augustness Fire-Subside peeped at her.

l: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely was the august child borne by Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess. He wedded his maternal aunt, Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, and begot four august children.

l: Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess was the younger sister of Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess. She nursed the august child and received a song from Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess to present to His Augustness Fire-Subside. She later became the wife of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely.

l: His Augustness-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: His Augustness-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears dwelt in the palace of Takachiho for five hundred and eighty years. His august mausoleum was likewise on the west of Mount Takachiho.

l: parturition, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Parturition began before the thatch of the parturition-hall was completed because Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess could not restrain the urgency of her womb. During parturition she entered her native shape, becoming a crocodile.

l: peeping at Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: Peeping at Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess occurred when His Augustness Fire-Subside stealthily looked at her during parturition. Afterward she felt ashamed, closed the sea-boundary, and returned to the Sea-Plain.

l: wedding of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely and Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The wedding of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely and Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess took place after Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess returned to the Sea-Plain. They begot four august children.

l: children of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Volume I (The Age of the Gods), Sect.
s: The children of His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely and Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess were His Augustness Five-Reaches, His Augustness Boiled-Rice, His Augustness August-Food-Master, and His Augustness Young-August-Food-Master. His Augustness Young-August-Food-Master was also called His Augustness Luxuriant-August-Food-Master and His Augustness Divine-Yamato-Ihare-Prince.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, later identified as Emperor Jim-Mu, progresses eastward from Himuka, defeats resisting forces, and establishes rule at Kashibara near Unebi. His elder brother His Augustness Itsu-se dies after being wounded in the battle with Nagasune-biko of Tomi. With guidance from the Great-High-Integrating-Deity, the cross-sword, and the eight-foot crow, His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko conquers and pacifies the Empire. After his death, His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi kills His Augustness Tagishi-mimi, and the imperial mausoleum is placed on the Kashi Spur by Mount Unebi.

l: His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He leaves Himuka and progresses eastward through Tsukushi, Agi, Kibi, Kumanu, Uda, and other places. He receives the cross-sword, follows the eight-foot crow, defeats resisting forces, establishes rule at Kashibara near Unebi, and fathers children with I-suke-yori-hime.

l: His Augustness Itsu-se, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He joins His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko in the eastward progress. After being wounded in the hand by Nagasune-biko of Tomi, he dies at the river-mouth of Wo, and his mausoleum is placed on Mount Kama in the land of Ki.

l: Emperor Jim-Mu, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: This title refers to His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, whose reign includes the eastward progress, the conquest and pacification of the Empire, and rule from Kashibara near Unebi. His august years are given as one hundred and thirty-seven.

l: His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is one of the three younger brethren threatened by His Augustness Tagishi-mimi. He takes the weapon from His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi and kills His Augustness Tagishi-mimi, after which he is called His Augustness Take-nuna-kaha-mimi and rules the Empire.

l: His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is instructed to kill His Augustness Tagishi-mimi but is unable to do so because his arms and legs tremble. He yields precedence to His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi and agrees to assist him as a priest.

l: His Augustness Tagishi-mimi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is the elder half-brother of the younger princes and weds the Empress I-suke-yori-hime after the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign. He plots to kill his three younger brethren but is killed by His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi.

l: Nagasune-biko of Tomi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He raises an army and waits to fight His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko after the latter reaches the haven of Shirakata. His forces wound His Augustness Itsu-se in the hand.

l: Takakurazhi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is a person of Kumanu who brings a cross-sword to the prostrate His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. He explains that the sword was sent down through the roof of his store-house according to a dream.

l: Ukashi the Elder Brother, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He attempts to turn back the eight-foot crow, prepares to attack His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, and builds a palace containing a pitfall. He is forced into the pitfall, dies there, and is cut in pieces.

l: Ukashi the Younger Brother, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He informs His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko of the elder brother's plot and thereby helps expose the trap. He presents a great banquet, which is bestowed on the august army, and is identified as the ancestor of the Water Directors of Uda.

l: His Augustness Ohokume, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is an ancestor of the Kume Lords and helps force Ukashi the Elder Brother into the pitfall. He later tells the Heavenly Sovereign about I-suke-yori-hime and communicates the Heavenly Sovereign's decree to her.

l: His Augustness Nigi-hayabi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He waits on His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko after hearing that the august child of the Heavenly Deity had descended from Heaven. He presents the heavenly symbols, respectfully serves him, and weds the Princess of Tomi.

l: I-suke-yori-hime, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is among seven beauteous maidens on the moor of Takasazhi and agrees to serve the Heavenly Sovereign. She bears His Augustness Hiko-ya-wi, His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi, and His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi, and later warns them through songs of His Augustness Tagishi-mimi's plot.

l: Great-High-Integrating-Deity, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He commands and teaches His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko not to progress further into the interior and sends the eight-foot crow from Heaven to guide him.

l: the august army, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It travels with His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and becomes prostrate after the appearance of the large bear at Kumanu. It recovers when the cross-sword is presented, participates in the fighting, and receives the banquet presented by Ukashi the Younger Brother.

l: Himuka, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is the place from which His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and His Augustness Itsu-se begin their eastward progress.

l: Kumanu, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is reached during the progress of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. A large bear appears from its mountain, causing the august army to faint, and Takakurazhi of Kumanu brings the cross-sword there.

l: Uda, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko reaches Uda after following the eight-foot crow and encountering Earthly Deities. Ukashi the Elder Brother and Ukashi the Younger Brother live there, and the place of Ukashi the Elder Brother's death is called Uda-no-Chihara.

l: Tomi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is associated with Nagasune-biko, who raises an army against His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. The Princess of Tomi is later wedded to His Augustness Nigi-hayabi.

l: Kashibara, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko dwells at the palace of Kashibara near Unebi after subduing the savage Deities and extirpating the unsubmissive people.

l: Mount Unebi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is near Kashibara, where His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko rules the Empire. The imperial mausoleum is on the Kashi Spur on its northern side.

l: the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is described as painfully uproarious, prompting the Heaven-Shining-Great-Deity and the Great-High-Integrating-Deity to send the cross-sword and direct action to pacify it.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is the realm whose government His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko seeks to carry on quietly by going east. After the savage Deities and unsubmissive people are subdued, he rules the Empire from Kashibara.

l: the eastward progress, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It begins when His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and His Augustness Itsu-se leave Himuka. It proceeds through several palaces and lands toward Yamato, involving battles, divine guidance, and the establishment of rule.

l: Itsu-se's death, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Itsu-se's death follows his wounding by Nagasune-biko of Tomi. He dies at the river-mouth of Wo after declaring that he has been struck by the wretched villain's hand.

l: the conquest and pacification of the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko accomplishes it by defeating Nagasune-biko's forces, overcoming the Ukashi brethren and the earth-spiders, and subduing the savage Deities and unsubmissive people.

l: the battle with Nagasune-biko, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Nagasune-biko raises an army against the advancing His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. During the fighting, His Augustness Itsu-se is pierced in the hand and later dies.

l: the slaying of Ukashi the Elder Brother, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Michi-no-Omi and His Augustness Ohokume compel Ukashi the Elder Brother to enter the palace he built as a trap. He falls into his own pitfall, dies, and is cut in pieces.

l: the slaying of Tagishi-mimi, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi kills His Augustness Tagishi-mimi after His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi fails to do so. The killing follows I-suke-yori-hime's warning about Tagishi-mimi's plot.

l: the cross-sword, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is sent down through the roof of Takakurazhi's store-house by the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity. Takakurazhi presents it to His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, after which the savage Deities of Kumanu are cut down.

l: the eight-foot crow, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is sent from Heaven by the Great-High-Integrating-Deity to guide His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko. It leads him to the lower course of the Yeshinu river and onward toward Uda.

l: the imperial mausoleum, Kojiki, Sect. XLIV.—Reign of the Emperor Jim-Mu (Part I.—His Progress Eastward, and Death of His Elder Brother) .. Sect. LIV.—Emperor Jim-Mu (Part XI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The mausoleum of His Augustness Itsu-se is on Mount Kama in the land of Ki. The mausoleum of His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko is on the top of the Kashi Spur on the northern side of Mount Unebi.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LV.—Emperor Sui-Zei.
s: Emperor Sui-Zei, also called His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi, dwelt at the palace of Takawoka in Kadzuraki and ruled the Empire. He wedded Kaha-mata-bime, ancestress of the Departmental Lords of Shiki, and they begot His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi. His august years were forty-five, and his mausoleum is on the Mound of Tsukida.

l: His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi, Kojiki, Sect. LV.—Emperor Sui-Zei.
s: Emperor Sui-Zei, called His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi, dwelt at the palace of Takawoka in Kadzuraki and ruled the Empire. He wedded Kaha-mata-bime and lived for forty-five years. His august mausoleum is on the Mound of Tsukida.

l: Kaha-mata-bime, Kojiki, Sect. LV.—Emperor Sui-Zei.
s: Kaha-mata-bime was ancestress of the Departmental Lords of Shiki. She wedded His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi and begot His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi.

l: Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi, Kojiki, Sect. LV.—Emperor Sui-Zei.
s: Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi was begotten by His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi and Kaha-mata-bime.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi dwelt in the palace of Ukiana at Kata-shiha and ruled the Empire. He wedded Akuto-hime and begot three august children, including His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo and His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko. His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo later ruled the Empire, while His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko had two Kings as children, including His Augustness Wa-chi-tsumi. His Augustness Wa-chi-tsumi dwelt in the palace of Miwi in Ahaji and had two daughters, and His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi’s august years were forty-nine.

l: His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: He dwelt in the palace of Ukiana at Kata-shiha and ruled the Empire. He wedded Akuto-hime and begot His Augustness Toko-ne-tsu-hiko-irone, His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo, and His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko. His august years were forty-nine.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: It was ruled by His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi. His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo afterwards ruled it.

l: Akuto-hime, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: She was the daughter of the Departmental Lord Haye and elder sister of Kaha-mata-bime. She wedded His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi and begot three august children.

l: His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: He was one of the three august children of His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi and Akuto-hime. He afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: He was one of the three august children of His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-de-mi and Akuto-hime. He had two Kings as children, including His Augustness Wa-chi-tsumi.

l: His Augustness Wa-chi-tsumi, Kojiki, Sect. LVI.—Emperor an-Nei.
s: He was a child of His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko and dwelt in the palace of Miwi in Ahaji. He had two daughters, Hahe-irone and Hahe-irodo.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LVII.—Emperor I-Toku.
s: Emperor I-Toku, also called His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo, dwelt in the palace of Sakahiwo at Karu and ruled the Empire. He wedded Princess Futo-ma-waka, also called Princess Ihi-bi, and begot Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine and Tagishi-hiko. His august years were forty-five, and his mausoleum was above the Vale of Manago by Mount Unebi.

l: His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo, Kojiki, Sect. LVII.—Emperor I-Toku.
s: Emperor I-Toku dwelt in the palace of Sakahiwo at Karu and ruled the Empire. He wedded Princess Futo-ma-waka and had two august children, Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine and Tagishi-hiko. His august years were forty-five, and his mausoleum was above the Vale of Manago by Mount Unebi.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LVII.—Emperor I-Toku.
s: The Empire was ruled by Emperor I-Toku, also called His Augustness Oho-yamato-hiko-suki-tomo.

l: Princess Futo-ma-waka, Kojiki, Sect. LVII.—Emperor I-Toku.
s: Princess Futo-ma-waka, also called Princess Ihi-bi, was wedded to Emperor I-Toku. She was the ancestress of the Departmental Lords of Shiki and was the mother of Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine and Tagishi-hiko.

l: His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine, Kojiki, Sect. LVII.—Emperor I-Toku.
s: His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine was begotten by Emperor I-Toku and Princess Futo-ma-waka. He was later the one who ruled the Empire.

l: His Augustness Tagishi-hiko, Kojiki, Sect. LVII.—Emperor I-Toku.
s: His Augustness Tagishi-hiko was begotten by Emperor I-Toku and Princess Futo-ma-waka. He was the ancestor of the Lords of Chinu, the Lords of Take in Tajima, and the Territorial Lords of Ashiwi.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: Emperor Ko-Sho, His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine, dwelt at the palace of Waki-no-kami in Kadzuraki and ruled the Empire. He wedded Her Augustness Princess Yoso-taho, younger sister of Oki-tsu-yoso, and begot His Augustness Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko and His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito. Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito afterwards ruled the Empire, while Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko became ancestor of numerous grandees, dukes, and rulers. Emperor Ko-Sho's august years were ninety-three, and his August mausoleum was on Mount Hakata at Waki-no-kami.

l: His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-wake-shine, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: Emperor Ko-Sho, identified as His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine, dwelt at the palace of Waki-no-kami in Kadzuraki and ruled the Empire. His august years were ninety-three, and his August mausoleum was on Mount Hakata at Waki-no-kami.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: The Empire was ruled by His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine from the palace of Waki-no-kami in Kadzuraki.

l: Princess Yoso-taho, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: Her Augustness Princess Yoso-taho was the younger sister of Oki-tsu-yoso, ancestor of the Chiefs of Wohari. She wedded His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine and bore two august children.

l: Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: His Augustness Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko was the elder of the two august children. He was the ancestor of the Grandees of Kasuga, Ohoyake, Ahata, Wonu, Kaki-no-moto, Ichihiwi, Ohosaka, Ana, Taki, Haguri, Chita, Muza, Tsunuyama, the Dukes of Ihitaka in Ise and Ichishi, and the Rulers of the Land of Chika-tsu-Afumi.

l: Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito was the younger of the two august children. He was the one who afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: ruling the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine ruled the Empire from the palace of Waki-no-kami in Kadzuraki. His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: marriage of Emperor Ko-Sho and Princess Yoso-taho, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine wedded Her Augustness Princess Yoso-taho, the younger sister of Oki-tsu-yoso, ancestor of the Chiefs of Wohari.

l: birth of the august children, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: The marriage of His Augustness Mi-ma-tsu-hiko-kawe-shine and Her Augustness Princess Yoso-taho produced His Augustness Ame-oshi-tarashi-hiko and His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito.

l: Mount Hakata, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: Mount Hakata was the location of Emperor Ko-Sho's August mausoleum, at Waki-no-kami.

l: August mausoleum of Emperor Ko-Sho, Kojiki, Sect. LVIII.—Emperor Ko-Sho.
s: Emperor Ko-Sho's August mausoleum was on Mount Hakata at Waki-no-kami.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LIX.—Emperor Koan.
s: Sect. LIX concerns Emperor Koan, identified as His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito. He dwelt at the palace of Akidzushima at Muro in Kadzuraki and ruled the Empire. He wedded his niece, Her Augustness Princess Oshika, and had two august children, including Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-futo-ni, who later ruled the Empire. His august years were one hundred and twenty-three, and his mausoleum was on the Mound of Tamade.

l: Emperor Koan, Kojiki, Sect. LIX.—Emperor Koan.
s: Emperor Koan is identified with His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito. He ruled the Empire, lived for one hundred and twenty-three years, and had his mausoleum on the Mound of Tamade.

l: Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito, Kojiki, Sect. LIX.—Emperor Koan.
s: Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito dwelt at the palace of Akidzushima at Muro in Kadzuraki and ruled the Empire. He wedded his niece, Her Augustness Princess Oshika, and begot Oho-kibi-no-moro-susumi and Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-futo-ni.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LIX.—Emperor Koan.
s: The Empire was ruled by His Augustness Oho-yamato-tarashi-hiko-kuni-oshi-bito. Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-futo-ni later ruled the Empire.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: Emperor Kō-Rei, His Augustness Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-futo-ni, dwelt at the Palace of Ihodo at Kuruda and ruled the Empire. His son Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru was the one who afterwards ruled the Empire. Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima and, making Harima the mouth of the road, subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi. Emperor Kō-Rei's august years were one hundred and six, and his mausoleum was at Umasaka at Kotawoka.

l: Emperor Kō-Rei, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: Emperor Kō-Rei dwelt at the Palace of Ihodo at Kuruda and ruled the Empire. His august years were one hundred and six, and his mausoleum was at Umasaka at Kotawoka.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: The Empire was ruled by Emperor Kō-Rei from the Palace of Ihodo at Kuruda. It was later ruled by his son Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru.

l: Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru was a son of Emperor Kō-Rei. He was the one who afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko together set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima and subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi. Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko was the ancestor of the Grandees of Kamu-tsu-michi in Kibi.

l: Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko and Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko together set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima and subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi. Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko was the ancestor of the Grandees of Shimo-tsu-michi in Kibi and of the Grandees of Kasa.

l: Harima, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: Harima was made the mouth of the road by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko as they subdued and pacified the Land of Kibi. They set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima.

l: Kibi, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: The Land of Kibi was subdued and pacified by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko, with Harima made the mouth of the road.

l: subjugation and pacification of the Land of Kibi, Kojiki, Sect. LX.—Emperor Kō-Rei.
s: The subjugation and pacification of the Land of Kibi was carried out by Oho-kibi-tsu-hiko and Waka-take-kibi-tsu-hiko. They set sacred jars at the front of the River Hi in Harima and made Harima the mouth of the road.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: Emperor Kō-Gen, His Augustness Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru, dwelt at Sakaki-bara at Karu and ruled the Empire. He had five august children, including Oho-biko and Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi, who afterwards ruled the Empire. Oho-biko’s descendants and those of Noble Take-Uchi are identified as ancestors of numerous Grandees, Chiefs, and Dukes. Emperor Kō-Gen’s august years were fifty-seven, and his mausoleum was on the mound in the middle of the Pool of Tsurugi.

l: Emperor Kō-Gen, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: Emperor Kō-Gen, also called His Augustness Oho-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-kuni-kuru, dwelt in the palace of Sakaki-bara at Karu and ruled the Empire. His august years were fifty-seven, and his august mausoleum was on the mound in the middle of the Pool of Tsurugi.

l: the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: The Empire was ruled by Emperor Kō-Gen. It was afterwards ruled by Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi.

l: His Augustness Oho-biko, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: Oho-biko was one of the august children of Emperor Kō-Gen. His children were Take-numa-kaha-wake and Hiko-inakoshi-wake, ancestors of the Grandees of Abe and the Butler Grandees.

l: Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi was one of the august children of Emperor Kō-Gen. He afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: the Noble Take-uchi, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: Noble Take-Uchi was begotten by Hiko-futu-oshi-no-makoto and Princess Yama-shita-kage. His children numbered nine, and they became ancestors of numerous Grandees, Chiefs, and Dukes.

l: august children of this Heavenly Sovereign, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: The august children of this Heavenly Sovereign numbered five Deities. They included Oho-biko, Sukuna-biko-take-wi-goro, Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-oho-bibi, Hiko-futu-oshi-no-makoto, and Take-hani-yasu-biko.

l: children of Noble Take-Uchi, Kojiki, Sect. XLI.—Emperor Kō-Gen.
s: The children of Noble Take-Uchi numbered nine, seven males and two females. They included the Noble of Hata-no-Yashiro, Noble Kose-no-Wo-Kara, Noble Soga no Ishikaha, Noble Heguri-no-Tsuku, Noble Kino-Tsunu, Princess Mato of Kume, Princess Nu-no-iro, Kadzuraki-no-Nagaye-no-sotsu-biko, and Noble Waku-go, who were ancestors of various Grandees, Chiefs, and Dukes.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: Emperor Kai-Kuwa ruled the Empire from the palace of Izakaha at Kasuga and fathered five august children, including Mima-kiri-biko-iniwe and King Hiko-imasu. King Hiko-imasu fathered eleven Kings, including King Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi, and his descendants became ancestors of various regional rulers and noble families. King Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi fathered Princess Hibasu, Princess Matonu, Princess Oto-hime, and King Mi-kado-wake. King Noble Okinaga fathered Princess Okinaga-tarashi, Sora-tsu-hime, and King Prince Okinaga, and his descendants included rulers of Tajima.

l: Emperor Kai-Kuwa, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: Emperor Kai-Kuwa, also called His Augustness Waka-yamato-ne-ko-hiko-ōho-bibi, dwelt in the palace of Izakaha at Kasuga and ruled the Empire. He fathered five august children, including Mima-kiri-biko-iniwe, King Hiko-imasu, and one Queen, and his august years were sixty-three; his mausoleum was at the top of the hill of Izakaha.

l: the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: The Empire was ruled by Emperor Kai-Kuwa from the palace of Izakaha at Kasuga.

l: Hiko-yumusumi, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: Hiko-yumusumi was the child of Emperor Kai-Kuwa and the Princess of Takanu. His children were King Oho-tsutsuki-tari-ne and King Sanugi-tari-ne, whose descendants included five Deities daughters.

l: Mima-kiri-biko-iniwe, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: Mima-kiri-biko-iniwe was the child of Emperor Kai-Kuwa and Her Augustness I-gaka-shiko-me. He later ruled the Empire.

l: King Hiko-imasu, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: King Hiko-imasu was the child of Emperor Kai-Kuwa and Her Augustness Oke-tsu-hime. He fathered eleven Kings through several marriages, and his descendants became ancestors of numerous Dukes, Lords, Chiefs, and regional rulers.

l: King Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: King Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi was the child of King Hiko-imasu and Okinaga-no-midzu-yori-hime, and was Prince of Taniha. He wedded the Lady Masu of Kahakami in Taniha and fathered Princess Hibasu, Princess Matonu, Princess Oto-hime, and King Mi-kado-wake.

l: King Noble Okinaga, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: King Noble Okinaga was the child of King Kami-me-ikadzuchi and Princess Takaki. He wedded the Princess of Takanuka in Kadzuraki and fathered Princess Okinaga-tarashi, Sora-tsu-hime, and King Prince Okinaga; he was also the ancestor of the Dukes of Homuji in Kibi and the Dukes of Aso in Harima.

l: King Hiko-imasu's children, Kojiki, Sect. LXII.—Emperor Kai-Kuwa.
s: King Hiko-imasu's children included King Ohō-mata, King Wo-mata, King Noble Shibumi, King Saho-biko, King Wo-zaho, Saho-bime, King Muro-biko, King Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi, King Midzuho-no-ma-wa-ka, King Kamu-oho-ne, Midzuho-no-i-ho-yori-hime, and Mimi-tsu-hime, as well as children from his marriage to Woke-tsu-hime. The text states that his children numbered eleven Kings and records the ancestry and descendants of many of them.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The unit concerns Emperor Sū-Jin's genealogies, reign, military campaigns, restoration of peace, and burial. His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe ruled from the Palace of Midzu-gaki, and His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi succeeded him. A great pestilence was ended through worship of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things, while rebellions led by King Take-hani-yasu were suppressed. The Empire was pacified, tribute was established, pools were made, and Emperor Sū-Jin's age and burial place were recorded.

l: His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He dwelt at the Palace of Midzu-gaki at Shiki and ruled the Empire. He wedded three women and begot twelve august children in all.

l: His Augustness Oho-biko, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He was the father of Her Augustness Princess Mimatsu and was sent to the circuit of Koshi. He later joined His Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku in suppressing King Take-hani-yasu's army, then proceeded to Koshi.

l: His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He was the child of His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe and Her Augustness Princess Mimatsu. He afterwards ruled the Empire.

l: great pestilence, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It arose during the reign of His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe, causing the people to die as if none would be left. It ceased altogether after the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things was worshipped and the Earthly Deities were established and honored.

l: Heavenly Sovereign, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The Heavenly Sovereign grieved over the great pestilence and received the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things in an august dream. He ordered Oho-tata-ne-ko to worship the Great Deity of Great Miwa and commanded other rites, after which the country was tranquil. He also directed military action against King Take-hani-yasu and received reports after the campaigns.

l: Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He appeared to the Heavenly Sovereign in an august dream and said that the pestilence was his august doing. He required worship by Oho-tata-ne-ko, after which the divine spirit did not arise and the land was tranquillized.

l: Oho-tata-ne-ko, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He was discovered in the village of Minu in Kafuchi and identified himself through a genealogy as a child of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things. He was made high priest to worship the Great Deity of Great Miwa on Mount Mimoro. He was also said to be the ancestor of the Dukes of Miwa and the Dukes of Kamo.

l: Iku-tama-yori-bime, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She was the wife of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things and the daughter of His Augustness Suwe-tsu-mimi. A divine youth came to her at night, and she became pregnant with Oho-tata-ne-ko.

l: Great Miwa, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It was the place whose Great Deity was worshipped by Oho-tata-ne-ko as high priest. The name Miwa was explained by the three twists of hemp remaining after Iku-tama-yori-bime followed the thread to the deity's shrine.

l: Mount Mimoro, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It was the mountain on which the Great Deity of Great Miwa was worshipped by Oho-tata-ne-ko.

l: Koshi, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His Augustness Oho-biko was sent there to carry out the Heavenly Sovereign's commands. He proceeded there after the suppression of King Take-hani-yasu's rebellion.

l: His Augustness Take-nuna-kaha-wake, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He was the son of His Augustness Oho-biko and was sent to the twelve circuits to the eastward to quiet unsubmissive people. He later met his father in Ahidzu.

l: Yamashiro, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: A young girl at the Pass of Hera sang of Prince Mima-ki-iri and warned of plotting and killing. King Take-hani-yasu, who dwelt there, raised an army and confronted the Imperial forces at the River Wakara.

l: King Take-hani-yasu, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He was the Heavenly Sovereign's half-brother and was suspected of plotting a foul act. He raised an army in Yamashiro, confronted the Imperial forces, failed to strike His Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku with an arrow, and was killed by Hiko-kuni-buku's arrow.

l: His Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He was the ancestor of the Grandees of Wani and was joined to His Augustness Oho-biko in the campaign against King Take-hani-yasu. He killed King Take-hani-yasu with an arrow, causing the opposing army to rout and flee.

l: River Wakara, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The River Wakara in Yamashiro separated King Take-hani-yasu's army from the forces of His Augustness Oho-biko and His Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku. The two armies confronted and challenged each other across it.

l: two opposing armies, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: They confronted each other with the River Wakara between them. After King Take-hani-yasu was killed, his army was routed, pursued, and cut down, while the Imperial forces completed the pacification.

l: the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The Empire was ruled by His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe and later by His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi. After the pestilence and military disturbances ended, the Empire was at peace and tribute was first levied.

l: people, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: They died in great numbers during the pestilence, as if none were to be left. After the pestilence ceased and the rebellions were suppressed, they flourished and the Empire was prosperous.

l: pacification of the Empire, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It was achieved through worship of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things, rites for the Earthly Deities, and campaigns against King Take-hani-yasu and other unsubmissive people. Afterward the commanders reported to the Heavenly Sovereign, and the Empire was at peace.

l: august mausoleum of Emperor Sū-Jin, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It was on the mound at the corner of the Yamanobe road.

l: Emperor Sū-Jin's reign, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: During his reign a great pestilence arose and was ended through religious rites. Military campaigns restored peace, tribute on men's arrow-notches and women's finger-tips was first levied, and the Pool of Yosami and the Pool of Sakawori at Karu were made.

l: Emperor Sū-Jin, Kojiki, Sect. LXIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part I.—Genealogies). .. Sect. LXVIII.—Emperor Sū-Jin (Part VI.—His Age and Place of Burial).
s: His august years were one hundred and sixty-eight. His august mausoleum was on the mound at the corner of the Yamanobe road.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: This unit concerns Emperor Sui-Nin, his genealogies, the conspiracy of King Saho-biko and Princess Saho-bime, and the birth and later speech of Prince Homu-chi-wake. It recounts King Saho-biko and Princess Saho-bime's deaths, Homu-chi-wake's worship of the Great Deity of Idzumo, and the establishment of several clans. It also describes Tajima-mori's return from the Eternal Land with the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree, followed by the death of Emperor Sui-Nin and the burial of Princess Hibasu.

l: His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Emperor Sui-Nin ruled the Empire from the palace of Tama-kaki in Shiki. He opposed the conspiracy of King Saho-biko and Princess Saho-bime, oversaw Prince Homu-chi-wake's upbringing and worship at Idzumo, and died at the age of one hundred and fifty-three.

l: King Saho-biko, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: King Saho-biko, elder brother of Princess Saho-bime, conspired against Emperor Sui-Nin and sought to rule the Empire with his younger sister. He made an eight times tempered stiletto and was later slain by Emperor Sui-Nin.

l: Princess Hibasu, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Princess Hibasu was a wife of Emperor Sui-Nin and the mother of several of his children. As Empress, she was buried in the mausoleum of Terama near Saki; the text does not explicitly describe her death.

l: His Augustness Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: His Augustness Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake was a son of Emperor Sui-Nin and Princess Hibasu. He later ruled the Empire.

l: Princess Saho-bime, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Princess Saho-bime was made Empress by Emperor Sui-Nin and was the younger sister of King Saho-biko. She revealed her brother's conspiracy, escaped to the rice-castle, and later followed him in death.
