l: Prince Homu-chi-wake, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Prince Homu-chi-wake was born while Princess Saho-bime was in the rice-castle and was named for being born during the burning of the castle. He was initially unable to speak, but later spoke after worship of the Great Deity of Idzumo.

l: Tajima-mori, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Tajima-mori was sent by Emperor Sui-Nin to the Eternal Land to fetch the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree. He returned after Emperor Sui-Nin had died and wailed and wept himself to death.

l: Idzumo, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Idzumo was the land where Prince Homu-chi-wake worshipped the Great Deity of Idzumo. It was also where the ancestor of its rulers prepared a temporary palace and food for the prince.

l: Eternal Land, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The Eternal Land was the country to which Tajima-mori traveled to obtain the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree.

l: Great Deity of Idzumo, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The Great Deity of Idzumo was identified through divination as the source of Prince Homu-chi-wake's affliction. After the prince worshipped this Deity, he gained the ability to speak.

l: rice-castle, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The rice-castle was built by King Saho-biko to await Emperor Sui-Nin's attack. Princess Saho-bime fled there, and Prince Homu-chi-wake was born during the castle's burning.

l: eight times tempered stiletto, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The eight times tempered stiletto was made by King Saho-biko and given to Princess Saho-bime so that she could kill Emperor Sui-Nin in his sleep. She lifted it three times but could not cut him.

l: Homu-chi-wake's birth, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Homu-chi-wake's birth occurred while Princess Saho-bime was in the rice-castle during the conflict with Emperor Sui-Nin. His name referred to his birth during the castle's burning and in the midst of fire.

l: conspiracy against Emperor Sui-Nin, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The conspiracy against Emperor Sui-Nin was devised by King Saho-biko, who urged Princess Saho-bime to kill the Emperor and rule the Empire with him. Princess Saho-bime disclosed the plan after she was unable to carry out the killing.

l: death of King Saho-biko and Princess Saho-bime, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: King Saho-biko was slain by Emperor Sui-Nin after the conflict at the rice-castle. Princess Saho-bime followed her elder brother in death.

l: Homu-chi-wake's speech, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Homu-chi-wake did not speak until he heard the cry of a high-flying swan and later still remained unable to speak. After worshipping the Great Deity of Idzumo, he spoke about the imitation green-leafed mountain in the river.

l: worship of the Great Deity of Idzumo, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Prince Homu-chi-wake was sent to worship the Great Deity of Idzumo with Prince Ake-tatsu and Prince Una-kami attending him. After the worship was completed, he became able to speak.

l: Tajima-mori's return from the Eternal Land, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Tajima-mori returned from the Eternal Land with eight portions of clubmoss and eight spears bearing the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree. By then Emperor Sui-Nin had died, so Tajima-mori divided the offerings between the Great Empress and the Emperor's mausoleum.

l: death of Emperor Sui-Nin, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: Emperor Sui-Nin died after reigning for one hundred and fifty-three years. His mausoleum was in the middle of the moor of Mitachi at Sugahara.

l: death of Princess Hibasu, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The text does not explicitly describe the death of Princess Hibasu. It states that she was buried in the mausoleum of Terama near Saki when she was the Great Empress.

l: fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree was brought from the Eternal Land by Tajima-mori. The text identifies this fruit as what is now called the orange.

l: swan, Kojiki, Sect. LXIX.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part I.—Genealogies) .. Sect. LXXV.—Emperor Sui-Nin (Part VII.—His Death and That of the Empress Hibasu.)
s: The cry of a high-flying swan prompted Prince Homu-chi-wake's first utterance. Emperor Sui-Nin sent Yamanobe-no-Ohotaka to pursue and catch the swan, which was eventually taken at the Estuary of Wanami.

l: Kojiki, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The unit concerns the reign and genealogy of the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, also called Emperor Kei-Kō, and the deeds, death, transformation, and descendants of His Augustness Yamato-take. His Augustness Wo-usu, later called Yamato-take, subdues the Kumaso bravoes, the Idzumo bravo, rulers in Sagamu, and various savage Deities and unsubmissive people during his eastern expedition. Yamato-take dies after suffering illness following his encounter with the Deity of Mount Ibuki, then becomes a white dotterel and is buried in several august mausoleums. The unit also records Emperor Kei-Kō’s age as one hundred and thirty-seven and gives the genealogy of Yamato-take’s descendants.

l: Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He dwells in the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku and rules the Empire. He has numerous children by several women, including His Augustness Wo-usu, His Augustness Yamato-take, and Prince I-ho-ki-no-iri, and his august years are one hundred and thirty-seven.

l: Empress Kei-Kō, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The text is headed by Emperor Kei-Kō and does not separately describe an Empress Kei-Kō.

l: His Augustness Yamato-take, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He subdues the Kumaso bravoes, the Idzumo bravo, rulers of Sagamu, and savage Deities and unsubmissive people in the East. He dies after illness following his encounter with the Deity of Mount Ibuki, then becomes a white dotterel and is buried.

l: His Augustness Wo-usu, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He kills his elder brother after being commanded to teach him his duty. He disguises himself as a young girl to kill the Kumaso bravoes and is thereafter praised as His Augustness Yamato-take.

l: Princess Ka-guro, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is the daughter of King Princess Sume-iro-oho-naka-tsu-hiko and becomes the wife of the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko, bearing King Oho-ye.

l: Yamato-take, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is the name by which His Augustness Wo-usu is praised after killing the Kumaso bravoes. He later undertakes campaigns in the East, dies after illness, and is transformed into a white dotterel.

l: Oto-hime, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is one of the maidens whom His Augustness Oho-usu weds instead of summoning to the Heavenly Sovereign. She is identified as the mother of King Oshi-kuro-no-oto-hiko.

l: Kumaso bravoes, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: They are two unsubmissive and disrespectful men in the West. His Augustness Wo-usu disguises himself as a young girl, enters their cave, and kills them.

l: Her Augustness Yamato-hime, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is Yamato-take’s aunt at Ise. She gives him an august upper garment and skirt for his disguise, and later gives him the Herb-Quelling-Sabre and an august bag before his eastern expedition.

l: Princess Miyadzu, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is the ancestress of the Rulers of Wohari. Yamato-take pledges to wed her, later returns to her house, and places his august sword in her house before departing for Mount Ibuki.

l: Yamato-take's Empress, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is the mother of Yamato-take’s august children and is among those who build his august mausoleum and pursue him after he becomes a white dotterel.

l: Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: She is Yamato-take’s Empress. She enters the sea in his place to still the waves, and Yamato-take later begets King Waka-take with her.

l: Deity of Mount Ibuki, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He appears in the form of a white boar and causes heavy ice-rain to fall on Yamato-take after Yamato-take says he will take him empty-handed. Yamato-take becomes ill after the encounter.

l: His Augustness Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: He is one of the children of Yamato-take and Princess Futaji-no-iri. He later rules the Empire.

l: Land of Great Yamato, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is described by the Kumaso bravo as having a man braver than themselves, namely Yamato-take.

l: Yamato, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: It is called the most secluded and delightful of lands in one of Yamato-take’s Land-Regretting Songs. The songs are also associated with the august interment of a Heavenly Sovereign.

l: Land of Kumaso, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Kumaso is the name used for the two bravoes whom Yamato-take is sent to take and slay. One of them gives Yamato-take the august name Yamato-take before being killed.

l: Ise, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: Yamato-take goes into the temple of the Great August Deity of Ise before beginning his eastern expedition and speaks with his aunt Yamato-hime.

l: Sagamu, Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI.—Empress Kei-Ko (Part I,—Genealogies) .. Sect. XCIII.—Emperor Kei-Kō (Part XVIII. His Age and Place of Burial).
s: The Ruler of Sagamu deceives Yamato-take by claiming that a violent Deity lives in a lagoon. Yamato-take survives the ruler’s attempt to burn him in a moor and kills the rulers of the land.
